title: Autopilot guide - autopilot can dispatch other autopilots
description:
If there's several tasks to do (eg in an epic, or when a bug or blocker is found) it would be nice if the autopilot could dispatch itself an autopilot, and the lower "layer" drives the specific task (with steps/beats).

Examples: 

Autopilot 1 is tasked with an epic, it sees 6 tasks, and three can be worked on in parallel. It dispatches autopilot 2A, 2B, and 2C. 2B hits an error so creates a ticket, and sends off autopilot C. Once 2A, 2B, and 2C complete (with 2B waiting on C), autopilot then dispatches an autopilot for each of the remaining tasks. It keeps an altitude "above" individual tasks.

If an autopilot is working on a task and finds a blocking bug, it can file a ticket for that bug then dispatch an autopilot to work on it, either in parallel, or it can wait for it to complete.

Each autopilot reports back up the chain the state of its descendants, as it does its current state.

The Observation page should be carefully thought though as this is a lovely visual space, with branches and nodes.

Given the ability to send follow ups, each autopilot can talk with the others, ask for clarifications, question certain things, etc, to keep things flowing as needed, prevent things for spiralling (or request human input as needed). Essentially acting as ideal managers.

One autopilot lives at user altitude, and coordinates the others at task altitude.

comments.body:
## This is now running as a live manual proof (2026-06-30 session)

We've been dogfooding exactly this shape: **Claude sits at user altitude and dispatches task-altitude autopilots back-to-back** (the LIN-826 "validation drive"). Each task gets its own autopilot run; the driver stays above individual tasks and only reacts to what reports up the chain. So the core LIN-813 loop — *a coordinator at user altitude, workers at task altitude, reporting up the chain* — is real and working today, not hypothetical.

What that surfaced (and what's now landed to make it solid):
- **Up-chain reporting** ("each autopilot reports back up the chain") = the `subscribe:true` wake edge (LIN-826). A child's stop boundary now wakes its parent with the outcome instead of the parent polling — incl. a `[pending]` "my part's done, the task isn't" pause (LIN-843). This is the literal substrate for "reports back up the chain the state of its descendants."
- **No more wedge** (LIN-831) and **warm in-session follow-ups** (the drip that lets a parent keep feeding/clarifying a child — "each autopilot can talk with the others"; warm-hold gap currently being closed as LIN-845).

## The sharper framing: it's a context-isolation pattern

The real win isn't just "autopilots spawning autopilots" — it's that **each task keeps its own context in its own session.** One autopilot doesn't have to grind every step of every task through a single context window. An epic with N subtasks becomes a driver that dispatches one focused autopilot per subtask, each carrying only its own task's context (research → plan → implement → review, with beats), while the driver holds the cross-task altitude. That's both a quality argument (no context dilution / no one session drowning in six tasks) and a cost/latency argument (no re-paging the whole epic per step).

## On parallel — "follow-up, or not?"

Honest read: the **comms primitives are already fan-out-shaped**, so parallel isn't architecturally blocked. A wake is just a dispatch addressed to the parent; one parent being woken by 2A/2B/2C is the same mechanism run three times — nothing in it is serial. So your "it seems to work?" instinct is well-founded.

But this session has deliberately run **serial** (one clean run at a time), so parallel is *unproven*, not *proven*. The real gates before trusting 2A/2B/2C concurrently are operational, not architectural:
1. **Multiple live consumers** draining the queue (today's drive leans on one).
2. **Workspace/run isolation** under concurrency (the per-`urlKey` isolation tracked as LIN-625 is the nearest existing concern).
3. **Driver coordination at altitude** — tracking N children's states, fan-in joins ("2B waits on C"), and not letting one stall block the batch. The Observation page (branches/nodes, as the description notes) is where this becomes legible.

Recommendation: keep landing the serial path first (it's the foundation and it's working), then do **one small, deliberate parallel validation** (e.g. an epic with 2–3 genuinely independent subtasks) rather than either assuming it works or deferring it indefinitely. If that one run holds, parallel is real; if it wobbles, it'll wobble on (1)/(2)/(3) above, which are nameable and fixable.

Scope this task first to autopilot dispatching autopilot so there's one ap per task to drive the steps, and one head ap.

File follow ups for the more advanced usage.
